what: The score combines generalized insertion cost, geometric attachment regret, demand urgency, and one-step capacity packing. The insertion term chooses the slot; subtracting depot distance counters the usual bias toward near-depot customers. Attachment compares the candidate’s nearest current-route node with its nearest other unassigned neighbor. Demand urgency protects large customers that may soon stop fitting, while projected residual waste mildly favors well-packed route closures. Each call costs O(|route| + |unassigned|) time and O(1) space.
why: Farthest-first route seeds benefit from growing coherent geographic clusters rather than immediately absorbing cheap near-depot nodes. The signed attachment term uses the remaining customer layout to avoid taking customers that have a substantially better future cluster, while the capacity terms address the strong demand pressure visible in small-capacity instances without solving a packing subproblem. The coefficients are scale-adjusted using mean remaining depot distance, so the rule is not tied to the representative coordinate ranges. It remains a greedy heuristic: nearest-neighbor attachment can misread elongated or interleaved clusters, and the one-step packing signal cannot detect combinations of several demands. Intra-route 2-opt can repair ordering but not a poor route assignment.
